analysis.one_liner: Stops drugmakers from switching patients to a reformulated drug to block cheaper generics.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 27-16 in September 2021, but the full House never voted on it before that Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug's patent is about to expire, some manufacturers make a minor change to the drug — a new dose, a new form — patent the new version, and pull the old one, so patients are moved to the still-protected product and cheaper generics never arrive. This bill tells the Federal Trade Commission that this practice, called product hopping, is an unfair method of competition, and gives the agency power to sue the manufacturer, unwind the profits, and make patients whole. The House committee in charge of the bill voted to advance it, but House leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs would get access to cheaper generics sooner, because drugmakers could no longer legally pull the old version or steer patients to a newly patented reformulation to reset the clock on their monopoly. Insurers, employers, and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid would also save on drug costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and insurers buying brand-name drugs

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes a manufacturer's withdrawal or destruction of an old drug, or conduct that steers patients to a reformulated version, prima facie evidence of an unfair method of competition, shifting the burden to the drugmaker to justify it [S3].
The FTC could enforce the ban through administrative proceedings or federal lawsuits, and could win disgorgement of profits or restitution, with a five-year window to seek recovery [S3].

The bill presumes a violation for both 'hard switches' (pulling the old drug) and 'soft switches' (disadvantaging the old drug in ways that block generic competition), with exemptions for legitimate safety reasons, supply disruptions, or pro-competitive justifications [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose the extended monopoly revenue that product hopping produces. Every month a generic is delayed can be worth tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in sales at brand-name prices, and the bill would shorten those timelines.

drawbacks.text: The bill could chill legitimate product improvements: manufacturers may hesitate to reformulate a drug even for real safety or efficacy reasons, because the bill creates a legal presumption against switches and lets the FTC override a manufacturer's justification if the agency finds the benefits do not outweigh the anticompetitive effects [S3].
Enforcement depends entirely on the FTC choosing to bring cases; the bill creates no private right of action for patients or payers, so relief would come only as fast as agency litigation moves [S3].
Savings only materialize if generics or biosimilars actually enter the market after a switch is blocked, which depends on separate market dynamics the bill does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — faster generic competition on drugs whose patents should have expired — is real and the FDA approval process already screens out unsafe reformulations, which limits the risk of chilling genuine improvements. The main honest objection is that bright-line presumptions can catch some legitimate business decisions, though the bill's justification and rebuttal provisions give manufacturers a path to defend them. On balance, the bill targets a well-documented tactic that keeps drug prices high, and its cost falls on the companies profiting from extended monopolies.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee voted 27-16 to advance the bill, but it was never reported to the House floor for a vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on April 28, 2021, joined by original cosponsors Reps. Jerrold Nadler, Ken Buck, and Carolyn Maloney, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1].
The committee held a markup on September 29, 2021, and voted 27-16 to order the bill reported in the nature of a substitute [S5].
No further action followed: the bill was never reported out of committee to the full House and never received a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].
The bill had bipartisan sponsorship, with five cosponsors — four Democrats and one Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the extension of their market exclusivity through product hopping remains legal under federal competition law, and patients kept paying brand-name prices for drugs that generic competitors could have sold for less.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drugmakers kept their extended monopolies

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored almost entirely by Democrats, with one Republican cosponsor among five; the committee's 27-16 vote to advance it was lopsided, but the record does not give the party breakdown of that vote.

industries.note: The bill would cut off a primary tactic for extending monopolies past patent expiry — pulling an old drug and steering patients to a newly patented reformulation — which can delay generics for years and keep patients paying brand-name prices. The industry's gain under the status quo is directly the public's added cost.

By blocking switches, the bill would let generic and biosimilar applications reach the market sooner instead of being rendered moot when the reference drug is pulled. Cheaper competition is the same outcome patients want.
Payers absorb much of the cost of extended brand-name monopolies through higher drug spending, so faster generic entry would lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs.
